lessons.name: The AND gate as arithmetic: AND a b = a · b over bits. Its truth table over (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1) is [0,0,0,1] — one only when both inputs are one.
lessons.why: The AND gate as arithmetic: AND a b = a · b over bits. Its truth table over (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1) is [0,0,0,1] — one only when both inputs are one.

lessons.name: The HALF-ADDER is correct: sum = XOR a b, carry = AND a b, and sum + 2·carry = a + b over every bit pair. The one-bit addition circuit, proven against its arithmetic meaning.
lessons.why: The HALF-ADDER is correct: sum = XOR a b, carry = AND a b, and sum + 2·carry = a + b over every bit pair. The one-bit addition circuit, proven against its arithmetic meaning.

lessons.name: NAND rebuilds NOT: NAND a a = 1 − a·a = 1 − a for a bit — tie a NAND's inputs together and it inverts. The first leg of NAND's universality.
lessons.why: NAND rebuilds NOT: NAND a a = 1 − a·a = 1 − a for a bit — tie a NAND's inputs together and it inverts. The first leg of NAND's universality.

lessons.name: The NOT gate as arithmetic: NOT a = 1 − a over a bit. Its truth table is [0,1] ↦ [1,0] — the one-input inverter, sealed exactly.
lessons.why: The NOT gate as arithmetic: NOT a = 1 − a over a bit. Its truth table is [0,1] ↦ [1,0] — the one-input inverter, sealed exactly.

lessons.name: The XOR gate as the axiom-free bitwise `lxor`: its truth table over the four rows is [0,1,1,0] — one exactly when the inputs differ. The difference detector, kernel-only.
lessons.why: The XOR gate as the axiom-free bitwise `lxor`: its truth table over the four rows is [0,1,1,0] — one exactly when the inputs differ. The difference detector, kernel-only.

lessons.name: XOR IS addition in ℤ/2: lxor a b = (a + b) mod 2 for bits. The difference gate and the parity sum are one arithmetic — the binary algebra folds back to the field of two elements.
lessons.why: XOR IS addition in ℤ/2: lxor a b = (a + b) mod 2 for bits. The difference gate and the parity sum are one arithmetic — the binary algebra folds back to the field of two elements.

lessons.name: NAND rebuilds AND: AND a b = NOT (NAND a b) = 1 − (1 − a·b) = a·b — a NAND followed by a NAND-inverter is an AND. The second leg.
lessons.why: NAND rebuilds AND: AND a b = NOT (NAND a b) = 1 − (1 − a·b) = a·b — a NAND followed by a NAND-inverter is an AND. The second leg.

lessons.name: The 2:1 MULTIPLEXER selects: mux s a b = (1−s)·a + s·b equals a when the select is 0 and b when it is 1, across all eight rows. Routing as arithmetic — the primitive every datapath is woven from.
lessons.why: The 2:1 MULTIPLEXER selects: mux s a b = (1−s)·a + s·b equals a when the select is 0 and b when it is 1, across all eight rows. Routing as arithmetic — the primitive every datapath is woven from.

lessons.name: The OR gate as arithmetic: OR a b = a + b − a·b over bits. Its truth table is [0,1,1,1] — zero only when both inputs are zero.
lessons.why: The OR gate as arithmetic: OR a b = a + b − a·b over bits. Its truth table is [0,1,1,1] — zero only when both inputs are zero.

lessons.name: NAND is FUNCTIONALLY COMPLETE for {NOT, AND, OR}: across every bit assignment, the three NAND reconstructions all hold at once — so a single gate type generates the whole basis. This is why digital chips are one repeated NAND.
lessons.why: NAND is FUNCTIONALLY COMPLETE for {NOT, AND, OR}: across every bit assignment, the three NAND reconstructions all hold at once — so a single gate type generates the whole basis. This is why digital chips are one repeated NAND.

lessons.name: NAND rebuilds OR: OR a b = NAND (NOT a) (NOT b) = 1 − (1−a)(1−b) = a + b − a·b — invert both inputs into a NAND. The third leg.
lessons.why: NAND rebuilds OR: OR a b = NAND (NOT a) (NOT b) = 1 − (1−a)(1−b) = a + b − a·b — invert both inputs into a NAND. The third leg.

lessons.name: The algebra is CLOSED on the bit: every primitive gate returns a value ≤ 1 for bit inputs — NOT, AND, OR, XOR all land back in {0,1}. Combinational logic never leaves 𝔹.
lessons.why: The algebra is CLOSED on the bit: every primitive gate returns a value ≤ 1 for bit inputs — NOT, AND, OR, XOR all land back in {0,1}. Combinational logic never leaves 𝔹.

lessons.name: De Morgan in gates: NOT (a AND b) = (NOT a) OR (NOT b), as 1 − a·b = (1−a) + (1−b) − (1−a)(1−b) over bits. The identity that lets a synthesiser push bubbles through gates.
lessons.why: De Morgan in gates: NOT (a AND b) = (NOT a) OR (NOT b), as 1 − a·b = (1−a) + (1−b) − (1−a)(1−b) over bits. The identity that lets a synthesiser push bubbles through gates.

lessons.name: THE SEAT ACCOUNTING, SEALED AFTER A LITERAL WAS FOUND WEARING ITS NAME. upgradeFirmware reported upgraded:true for every seat including the EMPTY one, so skipped was arithmetic on a constant and could not move off zero — an outcome published for an action never attempted. The cure is a three-answer domain, and this is the law it must satisfy: over the three seat kinds, the load outcome is UNMEASURED exactly when the seat is empty and LOADED otherwise, so the two outcomes partition the seats with nothing in a third bucket and nothing counted twice. The partition is walked over all 125 populations of up to four seats of each kind, not asserted at the one population this machine happens to have — a count of THIS host would be a reading on a Tuesday, and the ratchet record already names why that is not a theorem. NOT CLAIMED: that any seat holds hardware. The law is that the report cannot say it does when it does not.

lessons.name: The FULL-ADDER is correct: sum = XOR (XOR a b) cin, carry = (a+b+cin)/2, and sum + 2·carry = a + b + cin across all eight input rows. The cell every ripple-carry adder chains, proven exact.
lessons.why: The FULL-ADDER is correct: sum = XOR (XOR a b) cin, carry = (a+b+cin)/2, and sum + 2·carry = a + b + cin across all eight input rows. The cell every ripple-carry adder chains, proven exact.

lessons.name: ON A COMPLETE RESIDUE SYSTEM THE SHARD IS EXACTLY EVEN: 56 items over 14 lanes give every lane precisely 4, because 56 is a multiple of 14. The imbalance in the general case is therefore never structural — it is only the remainder, bounded by one item per lane, and it vanishes whenever the work divides.
lessons.why: ON A COMPLETE RESIDUE SYSTEM THE SHARD IS EXACTLY EVEN: 56 items over 14 lanes give every lane precisely 4, because 56 is a multiple of 14. The imbalance in the general case is therefore never structural — it is only the remainder, bounded by one item per lane, and it vanishes whenever the work divides.

lessons.name: THE LANES PARTITION THE WORK EXACTLY: summing what each of 14 lanes receives from 64 items returns 64 — nothing is lost between lanes and nothing is counted twice. This is WHY no coordination is needed. Residue routing is a partition of the input, so a lane can never need to ask another what it holds; the question a scheduler exists to answer cannot arise.
lessons.why: THE LANES PARTITION THE WORK EXACTLY: summing what each of 14 lanes receives from 64 items returns 64 — nothing is lost between lanes and nothing is counted twice. lessons.statement: (List.range 14).foldl (fun a l => a + ((List.range 64).filter (fun i => i % 14 == l)).length) 0 = 64

lessons.name: THE SHARD IS BALANCED TO WITHIN ONE ITEM, with no coordination and no measurement of load: 64 items over 14 lanes give every lane either 4 or 5, never fewer and never more. 64 = 4·14 + 8, so eight lanes take five and six take four. The balance is a property of the residue map itself, which is why it holds without any lane knowing what another is doing.
lessons.why: THE SHARD IS BALANCED TO WITHIN ONE ITEM, with no coordination and no measurement of load: 64 items over 14 lanes give every lane either 4 or 5, never fewer and never more. 64 = 4·14 + 8, so eight lanes take five and six take four. lessons.statement: ((List.range 14).map (fun l => ((List.range 64).filter (fun i => i % 14 == l)).length)).all (fun c => c == 4 || c == 5)
